pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–8 years

- **Topic:** Water Transport in Plants (investigation)

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y3 'Plants'):** 'investigate the way in which water is transported within plants' — a working-scientifically, first-hand INVESTIGATION; the canonical method is coloured water drawn up a cut stem (celery, pale flower).

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** honest note — no dedicated water-transport PE at this grade; it sits within plant-structure/function ideas (K-2-LS1-1 external structures) and later 5-LS1-1 (materials from water). This is primarily a UK Y3 investigation.

- **Operational details:** PROCEDURAL — the point is DOING and observing an investigation that makes an invisible process visible. Stand celery or a white carnation in coloured water; over hours the dye climbs and appears in the leaves/petals, evidencing that water travels UP from the cut base through the stem to the leaves and flowers. Slicing the stem afterwards reveals coloured dots/lines (the transport tubes), tying the observation to structure. The learning is threefold: (1) the OBSERVATION (colour reaches the top → water moved up); (2) the PATHWAY (roots/base → stem → leaves & flowers, an upward one-way route); (3) the METHOD itself — set up, wait, record over time, draw a labelled diagram of the path. Because it's slow and unseeable in real time, first-hand set-up plus time-lapse is ideal. Keep the mechanism simple: water moves up to the leaves (don't formalise xylem/transpiration — that's KS3). Guard against 'the stem sucks like a straw by mouth' — it's drawn up through fine tubes.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete, procedural). The child describes/sets up the coloured-water investigation, observes and records that colour reaches the leaves/petals, and draws a labelled diagram showing water's path base → stem → leaves/flowers — concluding water is transported upward through the stem.
bestPractices: Do it first-hand — celery or a white flower in dyed water — because the whole value is watching an invisible transport process reveal itself over hours.
Record over TIME (photos/drawings at intervals) so the slow upward creep of colour is captured as evidence, not just an end result.
Cut and examine the stem afterwards to show the coloured tubes, linking the observation to the transport structure.
Trace the PATH explicitly — base/roots → stem → leaves and flowers — and have the child draw and label it.
Keep the mechanism age-appropriate (water moves up through tiny tubes to the leaves); do NOT introduce xylem/transpiration terminology (KS3).
Use a split-stem or two-colour variation to deepen the investigation (each half draws its own colour) as an extension.
keyRepresentations: A stem/celery with dye visibly risen into leaves/petals — the canonical evidence image.
A stem cross-section showing coloured transport tubes as dots/rings.
A labelled path diagram: water from the base up the stem to leaves and flowers.
A timed photo/drawing series showing the colour climbing.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking water moves DOWN or in all directions rather than being drawn upward from the base to the leaves.
Believing the stem 'sucks' water like drinking through a mouth, rather than water rising through fine tubes.
Assuming leaves get their water directly (e.g. from rain/air) rather than via transport up the stem.
Thinking the colour appearing in petals is the flower 'making' colour rather than dyed water arriving there.
Not connecting the observation to structure — missing that the stem contains tubes that carry the water.
Expecting the process to be instant rather than taking hours.

learn.summary: Water transport in plants for ages 7-8 (UK DfE Year 3 'Plants'): a first-hand, working-scientifically investigation in which children stand celery or a pale white flower in dyed water, watch the colour climb over hours, and slice the stem to see the tubes that carried it. The learning is threefold: the OBSERVATION (colour reaches the top, so water moved up), the PATHWAY (base/roots to stem to leaves and flowers, an upward route) and the METHOD itself (set up, wait, record over time, draw a labelled diagram). Keep the mechanism simple (water moves up through tiny tubes to the leaves) and do not formalise xylem/transpiration, which belong to later secondary science. A screen simulation can compress the slow process and let children run variations, but it is an untested scaffold paired with the real experiment, which supplies the actual evidence. In US NGSS there is no dedicated water-transport performance expectation at this grade; it sits near plant structure/function (1-LS1-1, 4-LS1-1) and plants' need for water (2-LS2-1, 5-LS1-1).

activities.title: Real coloured-water investigation (celery or white flower)
feedback: If the learner expects the colour to stay only at the base, point to the dye in the leaf veins or petals: water climbed all the way up. Trace the continuous path base to stem to leaf together.
If the learner expects the stem to get wet on the outside, cut it crossways and show the coloured dots inside: water travels inside through specific channels, not over the surface.
If the learner expects an instant result, prompt 'what will you look at, and when?' so they build in waiting and a before/after comparison; the process takes hours.
If the learner says the flower is 'making' the colour, remind them the beaker water was dyed and that same colour has now arrived in the petals: it was carried there.
activities.rationale: The whole value of this topic is watching an invisible transport process reveal itself over time with real materials; doing and observing it first-hand, recording over time, and inspecting the stem matches the procedural, working-scientifically aim of the standard and ties observation to structure.
sourceClaims: DfE Y3 statutory: 'investigate the way in which water is transported within plants'.

Children often think a stem 'sucks' water like a mouth or that leaves get water directly, rather than water rising through tubes from the base; the coloured-water investigation makes the upward path visible.
learnerActions: Stand a stick of white celery with leaves on, or a pale white carnation, in a beaker of water dyed a bright colour (e.g. red or blue).
Before leaving it, write or say your plan: what will you look at, and when? Set up a before/after comparison and take a first photo or drawing.
Over several hours (or leave overnight), record what you see at intervals with photos or drawings, so the slow upward creep of colour is captured as evidence, not just a final result.
When the colour has risen, point out where the dye ended up (in the leaf veins / petals) and describe which way the water travelled.
Cut across the stem with scissors or a knife (with adult help) and use a hand lens to find the coloured dots or lines inside, the tiny tubes that carried the water.
Draw and label a diagram showing the path of the water: base/roots to stem to leaves and flowers.
activities.intendedInsight: Water is drawn upward from the base of the plant, through fine tubes inside the stem, all the way up to the leaves and flowers. Watching dyed water appear at the top is the evidence that this invisible, slow process happens.

activities.title: Compress and vary the investigation on screen
feedback: When the colour reaches the petals: 'coloured water arrived here, it travelled up from the base.'
When the stem is sliced: 'these tiny tubes inside carried the water up.'

For the split-stem prediction: if the learner expects one uniform colour, show each half drew up its own colour, giving a two-tone flower, because each half's tubes carried the dye from the beaker it was standing in.
activities.rationale: The process is slow and hidden, so a time-compressing, variable simulation may make the climbing dye and internal tubes visible and let children run comparisons (different colours, split stem) that are hard with a single real specimen. This is an untested scaffold: it shows and lets them vary the process, while the real dyed plant remains the evidence that it is true.
sourceClaims: Children often think a stem 'sucks' water like a mouth or that leaves get water directly, rather than water rising through tubes from the base; the coloured-water investigation makes the upward path visible.
learnerActions: Choose a specimen (white carnation or celery) and a dye colour, place it in the water, and drag a time slider forward to compress hours into seconds as the colour creeps up the stem and blooms into the petals or leaf edges.

Use a 'slice the stem' action to reveal the coloured dots inside (for a carnation stem these sit in a ring; in a celery stalk they sit in a curved row near the outer, ridged edge), the tiny tubes that carried the water, linking what you saw to the plant's structure.
Try a split-stem mode: put each half of the stem in a different colour and predict, then check, that the flower comes out two-toned.
Complete a label step: mark the water's path base to stem to leaves on the diagram.
activities.intendedInsight: Water moves up from the base through internal tubes to the leaves and flowers; varying the set-up (colours, split stem) shows the same pathway behaves predictably.

activities.title: Reference diagram: trace the path and the tubes
feedback: If the learner names the path out of order, re-anchor at the base: water enters low and rises, so the base comes first and the leaves/flowers last.
If the learner cannot locate the tubes, direct attention to the coloured dots in the cross-section.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal reference diagram clearly shows the path and the tubes and is a useful consolidating reference; it presents a finished result rather than letting the child run the investigation, so it supports but does not replace the first-hand work.
learnerActions: Tap or point to the dyed petal and say what it tells you ('coloured water arrived here, it travelled up').
Tap or point to the stem cross-section and name what carries the water ('tiny tubes carry water up').
Tap or point to the base and say what happens there ('water enters here').
Using the diagram, retell the whole path in order: base/roots to stem to leaves and flowers.
activities.intendedInsight: A labelled picture of the dyed plant and stem cross-section fixes the pathway and the location of the transport tubes as a memory aid after the investigation.

activities.title: Check understanding of method and pathway
feedback: If a learner orders observation before set-up, remind them you cannot observe before you have set it up and waited.
If a learner says water moves down or in all directions, point back to the dye reaching the top leaves/petals as evidence of an upward route.
If a learner predicts a single colour for the split stem, explain each half carries up its own dye, so the flower usually shows two tones, often in different parts of the petals.
activities.rationale: Ordering, path-drawing and targeted questions check whether the method and pathway are understood; these consolidate rather than enact the investigation, so they follow the hands-on work rather than standing in for it.
learnerActions: Put the investigation steps in the right order (set up specimen in dyed water, record over time, observe the colour risen, slice the stem to see the tubes).
Draw the water's route on a plant outline from base to stem to leaves.
Answer: which way does water move through the plant, and where does the colour appear first and last?
Predict: if you split the stem and stand each half in a different colour, what will the flower look like?
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can state the direction of movement (upward), the ordered pathway, and the role of the internal tubes, and can predict a variation.

constraints: This is a PROCEDURAL, first-hand investigation: the core learning is doing, waiting, observing and recording over time, so a real celery/carnation experiment should anchor the topic.
Keep the mechanism age-appropriate: water moves up through tiny tubes to the leaves. Do NOT introduce xylem or transpiration terminology, which belongs to later secondary science.
Guard against 'the stem sucks water like drinking through a mouth': water is drawn up through fine tubes, not sucked by a mouth.
The process takes hours; build in waiting and interval recording rather than expecting an instant result.

A screen simulation is an untested scaffold that compresses time and allows variations and a view of hidden tubes; it does not supply the first-hand evidence and should be paired with the real experiment.
A reference diagram and check-style questions present or review the finished result; they consolidate but do not substitute for setting up and observing the investigation.

Cross-section appearance depends on the specimen (carnation shows a ring of dots, celery a curved row of dots near the outer, ridged edge of the stalk); read the real cut as it actually appears rather than assuming a fixed pattern.
Cutting the stem needs adult supervision when a knife or scissors is used.
US NGSS has no dedicated water-transport performance expectation at this grade; this is primarily a UK Year 3 investigation.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The OpenLearn source (misconceptions; coloured-water investigation makes the upward path visible) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its specific claims as unconfirmed even where cited in sourceClaims, including where it is reused for the simulation activity to identify the same misconception.

The source phrasing 'water was pulled all the way up' and references to vascular bundles reflect real xylem/transpiration mechanisms not taught at this level; activities deliberately keep to 'water moves up through tiny tubes' per the stated KS3 boundary. The fuller mechanism is noted here only for context.

The original recommendation leaned strongly on the simulation as 'ideal'; this rewrite retains it as a scaffold and restores the first-hand experiment as the primary activity, consistent with the PROCEDURAL type and the standard's working-scientifically intent.

The 'conversation adds nothing' and '3D adds nothing/adds cost without revealing anything' judgements from the source are catalog-fit opinions, not established efficacy claims, and have not been propagated as universal laws.

Cross-section appearance depends on the specimen: carnation (dicot) shows a ring of dots while celery shows scattered bundles; the on-screen 'ring of dots' is an approximation and the real cut should be read as it actually appears.

probeDeeper: Where exactly did the red water end up — and what does that tell you about the direction water travels?
When you cut the stem, what did you see inside? What are those coloured tubes for?
Which part of the plant took the water in first, and which got it last?
If you split the stem and stood each half in a different colour, what would you predict?
assess.correctAnswer: Stands the celery in the red water, waits, and observes the red colour travelling UP the stem into the leaves; cutting the stem reveals red-stained tubes (vascular bundles) running through it. Concludes water travels from the bottom (roots end) UP the stem to the leaves, through tubes inside the stem. A good performance sets it up as a tracked observation and reads the path from root-end to leaves.

errorPatterns.pattern: water stays in the roots/bottom and doesn't travel up to the leaves
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point to the red in the leaf veins — water climbs all the way up. Trace the continuous path base→stem→leaf together.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: expects the red colour only at the base; surprised to find it in the leaves

errorPatterns.pattern: water soaks up the outside of the stem, not through tubes inside
errorPatterns.nextMove: Cut the stem crossways to reveal the red-stained tubes — water travels INSIDE through specific channels, not over the surface.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: doesn't cut/inspect the stem, or expects surface wetting rather than internal channels

errorPatterns.pattern: runs it as a one-off with no wait/observation plan (procedural lapse)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach transport — prompt 'what will you look at, and when?' so they build in waiting and a before/after comparison.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: expects an instant result, or doesn't leave time / doesn't plan what to look for

responseLevels.gap: Expects water to stay low or wet the outside; doesn't inspect the stem; can't trace a path.
responseLevels.full: Sets up a tracked observation, shows dye risen into the leaves and stained tubes inside a cut stem, and describes water travelling up through internal channels from the root-end to the leaves — predicting the split-stem two-colour result.
responseLevels.partial: Observes the colour rising and states water goes up, but doesn't connect it to internal tubes or lay out a clear root→stem→leaf path — result seen without the mechanism.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a stick of white celery (leaves on), a beaker of water dyed bright red, a knife/scissors and a hand lens. Say: 'Set this up to find out HOW water moves through the plant, leave it, then show me what you found and where the water went. You can cut the stem to look inside.' Watch how they set it up, what they observe, and how they trace the path — don't tell them what to expect.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Doing it (not describing it) reveals whether the child expects water to travel UP through internal tubes to the leaves, or holds that water just 'sits in the roots' / soaks the outside. The dyed water makes the invisible path visible; watching the setup and the where-did-it-go reading exposes the mental model.
